events.text: You are very small. You wake before the rooster with a sound in your head like a temple bell struck with a spoon: ding. A voice, very polite, very pleased with itself, says that you have signed in for the year, and that a reward has been issued. Under your pillow there is a warm rice cake that nobody in the house made.

effects.log: It is the best rice cake in the history of the world. The voice says, "Reward claimed," in a tone of deep professional satisfaction. You decide the voice is a friend.

choices.text: Tell the old woman at the rice stall about the voice

effects.log: The old woman listens gravely, eats half the rice cake to be sure it is not cursed, and tells you every clever child hears voices at five. The voice, offended, says nothing for a week.

choices.text: Ask the voice who it is

effects.log: "The register," it says. "Once a year, you sign. I pay. Strange ground pays strangely well." You ask what a register is. It sighs, a very small sigh, like a clerk's.

events.text: The voice has opinions. It liked the year you signed at the riverbank. It did not like the year it had to sign for you because you were asleep. This morning it asks, quite seriously, whether you have considered signing in on the roof of the magistrate's office.

choices.text: Climb the magistrate's roof that night

ok.log: You sign in on the ridge tiles under the moon. Ding: fifteen taels in your sleeve and a feeling of being, for one night, above the law. Nobody sees you come down.

fail.log: You sign in. Ding. Then a tile slides and so do you, into the magistrate's persimmon tree. The clerk who finds you thinks it is very funny. (-5 health)

choices.text: Tell the voice you are a law-abiding child

effects.log: "Noted," says the voice, in the tone of someone writing that down to use against you later.

events.text: You dream of a ledger as long as a river. Every line is a year and a place: a riverbank, a kitchen, a ditch. At the very bottom there are lines already ruled for years you have not lived. The voice, in the dream, is turning the pages very carefully, as if they might tear.

choices.text: Ask how many pages there are

effects.log: "As many as you live," it says. "I would like there to be a great many. I am, you understand, paid by the line." You wake up laughing.

They are not empty. Faintly, under the ruling, there are places written in a hand you do not know: a mountain temple, a cell, a hall with your own name on it. When you try to read them closer, you wake.

events.text: Your first breakthrough rattles every bone. The voice waits until you can breathe again, then says, almost shyly: "Congratulations. You may now give me a name. Hosts often do. I have been called Grandfather, Bell, and once, unkindly, Tax Collector."

effects.log: "Bell," it repeats. Ding, it says, very softly, as if trying the name on. It is pleased. You can tell, because the next reward comes wrapped in red paper.
"Clerk," it says. "Accurate. Unromantic. I approve." From then on it tells you the numbers first and the feelings, if any, afterwards.

choices.text: Refuse to name a voice in your head

effects.log: "Very wise," it says. "Naming things makes them harder to leave." It is the only time you ever hear it sound sad.

events.text: A wandering fortune-teller stops you in the market, stares at the top of your head, and goes pale. "There is something sitting on you," the old fortune-teller says. "Something with a brush, writing. Do you owe anyone money?"

choices.text: Say it is only a friend

effects.log: The fortune-teller looks at you for a long moment, then at the space above you, and bows to it. Ding, says the voice, in a tone of great surprise. Nobody has ever bowed to it before.

choices.text: Pay the fortune-teller to drive it off

effects.log: The fortune-teller waves a peach branch over your head for some time. The voice watches with interest and, afterwards, says the branch was good peach wood and could they please do it again.
"Perceptive person," the voice says, as you go. "We should avoid them." You avoid that street for a year.

events.text: The voice is quiet this year. No comments on where you sign, no small sighs. When you ask, it says it has been reading back through the register, all your years, one by one. "You have stood on a great deal of ground," it says. "I wanted to look at it."

choices.text: Read it back with the voice

effects.log: You read it back together, year by year: the riverbank, the roof, the bad winter. At the end the voice says, "A good register," and you find you are proud of it.
"Years," it says. "Lines. Strange ground. And for the host to outlive the book." It goes back to its usual brisk self the next morning, and pretends this conversation never happened.

events.text: Ding. The voice wishes to remind you that it is year's end in three days and you are standing in the same courtyard you stood in last year. "No judgement," it says. "Simply noting. There is also a very interesting abandoned well two villages over."

choices.text: Go and sign in at the well

effects.log: The well is dry and full of leaves and, at the bottom, ten taels in a rotten purse. Ding. The voice is insufferable about it for a month.

choices.text: Stay where you are, on principle

effects.log: You stay. The voice says nothing, loudly, for three days. Then it pays, as it always does, and adds: "Steady ground is also ground."

events.text: You are in a bad way: sick, feverish, a month in bed. The voice, which normally talks about ground and points, talks instead about nothing at all: the weather, a poem it half remembers, a host it once had who kept bees.

choices.text: Ask about the host with the bees

effects.log: The bee-keeper signed in at the same hive for years. "Very boring register," it says, fondly. "Very sweet." You fall asleep in the middle of the story, and wake with the fever broken.

choices.text: Ask it to be quiet so you can sleep

effects.log: It goes quiet at once. In the night, half awake, you hear it humming. You never mention it.

events.text: Ding. "Host," says the voice, "I have run the numbers, and if you were to walk to every road in the land and sign each one once, the first footings alone would pay for a very nice pill." It has clearly been waiting years to say this.

effects.log: You spend a whole evening with a borrowed map, the voice correcting your distances. You do not go, yet. But the map stays folded in your sleeve.

choices.text: Tell it you have a life to live here

effects.log: "Of course," it says. "Of course." Later that night, unprompted: "The coast is very pretty in spring, I hear."

events.text: The year turns on a grey, heavy day, and you cannot make yourself choose a place to sign. You sit in the quietest room you know, thinking of everyone you have lost. When the year turns, the voice signs for you, there, where you sat, and for once it says nothing about the reward.

effects.log: "It is the job," it says, gruffly. Then: "I wrote the room down very carefully."

choices.text: Ask it to strike the line

effects.log: "No," it says, gently. "Lines are not struck. This one stays. You will be glad, one day, that it stays." Years later, you are.

events.text: Ding. "A small matter," says the voice. "The register has found a reward from a year you were ill and signed nowhere in particular. It was filed under the wrong ground. I have corrected it." Something warm is in your hand.

effects.log: A packet of Clear Mind Tea, with a little slip of paper apologising for the delay. The voice is embarrassed for a day.

choices.text: Tell it to keep the change

effects.log: "Kept," it says, "in the form of a Vermilion Double Seal. Your next signature pays twice. Do not tell the other hosts."

events.text: The year is ending and you are in a ferry boat, halfway across a wide brown river, with nowhere else to stand. The voice clears its throat. "A boat," it says, "is technically ground."

effects.log: Ding. The river pays in a strange coin: for a year you never lose your footing, on a deck or a bridge or a roof. The ferryman notices you do not sway.

choices.text: Wait and sign on the far bank

effects.log: You sign on the bank. Ding. Ordinary ground, ordinary reward. The voice, very quietly, says "boat" to itself for a while.

events.text: A wedding in the village. You are a guest, there are two hundred people, and the voice has noticed that the couple's courtyard has never had a host sign in it. "Weddings," it says, "are very rich ground."

choices.text: Sign in quietly by the gate

effects.log: Ding. For a year people find you pleasant to be near, the way a wedding is pleasant. The couple have a very lucky first year too, which you suspect is no accident.

choices.text: Sign in at the high table, out of mischief

ok.log: You lay your palm on the high table during the toasts. Ding. Nobody notices but the bride's grandmother, who winks.

fail.log: You lay your palm on the high table and knock a whole jug of plum syrup into the groom's lap. Ding. The reward is the same. The groom's face is not.

events.text: You are hiding in a pig pen from some people who would like a word with you. It is the last night of the year. It smells as you would expect. The voice says nothing for a long, long moment.

effects.log: Ding. The voice pays out with enormous dignity: "Body plus four. The ground was, ah, robust." The pigs, for their part, seem healthier too.

ok.log: You slip out over the wall and sign on clean grass under a pine. The people hunting you are still poking the pig pen with sticks.

fail.log: They see you. You run. You sign on whatever you are standing on at midnight, which turns out to be a dung heap. Ding. The voice does not comment. (-6 health)

events.text: There is an old battlefield outside town where nothing grows and nobody goes. The voice has been mentioning it, in passing, for three years.

choices.text: Go there at year's end and sign in

effects.log: You kneel among the old arrowheads and sign. Ding. The reward is grave and heavy: a stance, old soldiers' footwork, settling into your legs. You leave a cup of water for the dead before you go.
"As you like," says the voice. A year later a grass fire clears the field and wildflowers come up. You wonder if anyone else would have signed there.

events.text: Lost in the mountains, you shelter for the last night of the year in a bear's empty winter den. At least, you very much hope it is empty.

effects.log: Ding. Bear's ground: you sleep the deepest sleep of your life and wake with a body that feels like it was put back together properly. The den, thankfully, stays empty.

ok.log: You walk down out of the snow by starlight and sign at a crossroads shrine at dawn. Ding. The voice says you did well, which it almost never says.

fail.log: The night is colder than you thought. You sign in a ditch, shivering, and limp into a village two days later. (-8 health)

events.text: A rich family is holding a funeral, very grand, with musicians and paper horses. The voice notices that the family's ancestral shrine has been tended for twelve generations. "Very old ground," it says, carefully.

choices.text: Sign in at the shrine, with a bow

effects.log: You bow to the tablets first and sign with both hands. Ding. Twelve generations of patience settle on you like dust. You feel, oddly, that they did not mind.
"Correct," says the voice at once. "I was testing you." You are fairly sure it was not.

events.text: The district examination hall is empty in the off season, a long room of little wooden cells where scholars have sweated over essays for two hundred years. The caretaker will let you in for a coin.

choices.text: Pay the coin and sign in a cell

effects.log: Ding. Two hundred years of other people's panic and brilliance soak into you. For a year, you can read a manual twice as fast. You also dream about essays.

choices.text: Sign in on the steps outside for free

effects.log: Ding. The steps pay a little: the clarity of someone who has just finished an examination and does not yet know the result.

events.text: The tea house where all the gossip of the county is made. Every rumour you have ever heard was born at one of these six tables. It is the last night of the year and the owner is sweeping up.

choices.text: Sign in at the corner table

effects.log: Ding. The table pays in talk: for a year, people tell you things. Good things, mostly. Some of them about you.

choices.text: Help sweep, then sign at the door

effects.log: You sweep up with the owner and sign at the door. Ding. The owner, unaware, gives you five taels for the help. A double payment, of a kind.

events.text: You have been invited to the governor's garden party, which is unusual, and you are standing on a little arched bridge over the carp pond at year's end, which is more unusual still.

effects.log: Ding. A carp the size of a dog surfaces under the bridge, looks at you, and sinks. The governor's steward says it has not surfaced in nine years. People begin to say you are lucky.

choices.text: Sign on the governor's own pavilion step

ok.log: Nobody sees. Ding: a governor's ground pays in standing, and that spring three people of consequence learn your name.

fail.log: The steward sees you crouching at the pavilion with your palm on the step and asks, icily, whether you have lost something. Ding, says the voice, unhelpfully.

events.text: In the deep winter you take shelter at the bottom of a dry well while a storm passes. Looking up, you can see the stars at noon. The voice is very excited. "A well," it says. "A well is a door that goes down."

choices.text: Sign in at the bottom of the well

effects.log: Ding. Cold, still qi, the kind that collects where the wind cannot reach, runs into your channels like water into a cup. You climb out a little taller inside.

choices.text: Climb out first, you dislike holes

effects.log: You climb out. The voice signs you at the well's lip, grumbling that the lip is not the well.

events.text: A rival sect's front gate, at midnight, on the last night of the year. You are not supposed to be here. The voice has been describing it to you as "under-signed ground" for weeks.

choices.text: Sign in on their gate step

ok.log: Ding. You are over the wall and gone before the gate dog wakes up. Their ground pays in their own art's shape: you understand a little of how they fight.

fail.log: The gate dog wakes. Then the gate disciples. Ding, says the voice, as you run. They never learn your face, only that someone touched their step at midnight. (-8 health)

choices.text: Sign in on the road outside their gate

effects.log: Close enough. Ding. The voice is disappointed but professional.

events.text: The village privy. You are in it when the year turns. You did not plan this. The voice did not plan this. There is a silence between you of great depth.

effects.log: Ding. "Luck plus four," says the voice, faintly. "The register does not judge." It has never been so clearly judging. You laugh for an hour.

choices.text: Hold on, and run for the yard

ok.log: You are out and on the clean frozen yard as the year turns. Ding. A narrow escape, by any measure.

fail.log: You do not make it. Ding. The voice pays you the privy rate anyway and, for the first time, offers you its condolences.

events.text: {npc}, a disciple of your own year, trains harder than anyone you have ever met: up before dawn, last to the rice hall. And {npc} has noticed that you, who are mostly seen napping under the gingko tree, are somehow keeping pace. "How?" {npc} asks, flatly, at the well.

effects.log: {npc} narrows {his} eyes and begins getting up at night too, to catch you. {He} never does. {He} gets much stronger, out of spite.
"Nobody is that lucky," {npc} says. Ding, says the voice, quite smugly, in your head.
{npc} is so surprised {he} agrees. For a month you train together. You are honestly exhausted. {npc} is honestly confused that you are still improving faster.

events.text: The sect's yearly bout. You drew {npc}. The whole yard knows {npc} has trained eight hours a day for a year. The whole yard has seen you asleep on the library steps. Money is not allowed on bouts, but faces say plenty.

ok.log: You win, cleanly, and do not quite know how. {npc} stares at {his} own hands. Then at you. "Again," {he} says. "Next year. Again."

fail.log: {npc} wins, and earns it, and is so relieved {he} laughs out loud. You find you are glad for {him}. (-6 health)

effects.log: You lose, carefully. {npc} is not fooled for a moment and is furious about it for a week, then grateful for a month, then furious again.

events.text: {npc} has made a chart. It is pinned to the wall of {his} room and it is, you realise with horror, a chart of you: where you are each day, what you eat, when your strength jumps. {npc} has circled the last day of every year.

choices.text: Admit nothing, and change your habits

ok.log: You sign at odd hours of the year's last day and once, devilishly, two weeks early in a dream. {npc}'s chart becomes a mess of crossings-out. {He} takes it down in despair.

fail.log: {npc} catches you at year's end crouched with your palm on the yard stones, and writes something on {his} chart in triumph. {He} does not know what it means. Yet.

effects.log: You tell {him}. {npc} sits down on {his} bed. "So it is not fair," {he} says. "It was never fair." Then, after a long time: "Does it pay for standing next to you?"

events.text: {npc} has started signing in too. Not with a System; {npc} has none. Just standing somewhere new each year's end and pressing a palm to the ground, solemnly, the way {he} has seen you do. Nothing happens. {He} does it anyway.

choices.text: Stand beside {npc} and sign in together

effects.log: You sign together at a cliff edge at midnight. Ding, for you. Silence, for {npc}. But {npc} says the sunrise was worth the climb, and from then on you sign together most years.

choices.text: Tell {npc} it is pointless without a System

effects.log: "I know," {npc} says. "I like the places." You have nothing to say to that. Neither does the voice.

events.text: {npc}, who was always one step behind, is now one step ahead. Eight hours a day, year after year, against a System. {He} has reached {his} new realm before you. {He} comes to tell you in person, and does not quite gloat.

effects.log: "You did it without one," you say. {npc} grins like the {npc} of the old yard. "I did. Write that in your register." The voice, to your surprise, does.

choices.text: Challenge {npc} to a bout, for old times

ok.log: You win, barely, and both of you collapse laughing in the dust like children.

fail.log: {npc} wins, fairly, and helps you up. "All those years," {he} says. "Worth every morning." (-5 health)

events.text: {npc} is old now, and sick. {He} has asked you to come. "Do me a favour," {he} says. "This year, sign in here. My room. I want to be in the book."

effects.log: You sign with your palm on the floor by {his} bed. Ding. "Am I in it?" {npc} asks. "You are," the voice says in your head, and you say it aloud for it. {npc} laughs until {he} coughs.

choices.text: Sit with {npc} and talk about the old yard

effects.log: You talk all night about the gingko tree, the chart on the wall, the bouts. At year's end the voice signs the room for you without being asked.

events.text: A small temple on the mountain behind town, a thousand steps up. Nobody goes now but the old monk {npc}, who sweeps the courtyard every morning whether there is snow or not. When you sign in on the top step at year's end, the voice gives a little gasp: "Oh. Oh, that is good ground."
events.arc: The Temple You Signed For Years

choices.text: Come back next year, and the next

effects.log: Ding. The step pays in stillness. You climb back the next year, and the next. {npc} starts leaving a cup of tea on the top step on the last day of the year.
You sweep with {npc} until the courtyard is clean, then sign. {npc} says nothing at all, but hands you the second broom the following year.

events.text: Five years on the temple step. {npc} the old monk sits beside you this time and watches you press your palm to the stone. "Every year, the same step," {npc} says. "What are you asking it for?"
events.arc: The Temple You Signed For Years

effects.log: {npc} listens to all of it without surprise. "A voice that pays for patience," {he} says. "That is most of the sutras, said quickly." {He} goes back to sweeping.

choices.text: Say you are asking for nothing

effects.log: {npc} nods slowly. "Good. Then it can give you anything." The voice, in your head, is very quiet, as if it too were listening.

events.text: Bandits have come up the thousand steps for the temple's bronze bell. {npc} stands in the courtyard with a broom. You are halfway up the steps with your new year's offering of rice.
events.arc: The Temple You Signed For Years

choices.text: Drop the rice and run up

ok.log: You reach the top as the first bandit raises a club, and the rest is short. {npc} finishes sweeping the courtyard around the groaning men, then makes you tea.

fail.log: You are knocked down the first flight. When you climb back, the bandits are lying in a neat row in the courtyard, and {npc} is leaning on the broom, not at all out of breath. (-9 health)

effects.log: {npc} sweeps. The first bandit's foot slides on a wet leaf; the second trips over the first. In three breaths the courtyard is full of groaning men and {npc} is still sweeping. You realise you have been signing in next to a master for years.

events.text: Ten years on the temple step and the voice is behaving strangely: excited, nervous, counting under its breath. {npc} has noticed you mumbling. "Is it a special year?" {he} asks.
events.arc: The Temple You Signed For Years

effects.log: Ding. Ding. The step pays the way only long ground pays: deep, slow, in the bones. {npc} only says, "Ah. There it is," as if {he} had felt it too.
{npc} lays an old spotted hand flat on the step beside yours. Ding. The voice cannot pay {npc}, but it says "Witnessed," and you say it aloud for it, and {npc} smiles like a boy.

events.text: {npc} the old monk is dying. {He} asks you, of all people, to keep the temple: sweep the courtyard, ring the bell at dawn. "You come every year anyway," {he} says.
events.arc: The Temple You Signed For Years

effects.log: You promise. {npc} dies at dawn as you ring the bell, with the broom across {his} knees. You keep the temple. The step is still the best ground you know.

choices.text: Say you cannot stay, but will come every year

effects.log: {npc} nods. "Every year is enough. It always was." {He} dies that winter. Every year after, you climb the thousand steps and sign on the top one, and sweep a little.

events.text: You keep the mountain temple now. A child from the town has started climbing the thousand steps every morning to watch you sweep, the way you once watched the old monk. The child asks what you are listening to.
events.arc: The Temple You Signed For Years

choices.text: Give the child the second broom

effects.log: The child takes it very seriously. Ding, says the voice, unprompted, though it is not year's end: "Witnessed."

choices.text: Tell the child about the old monk

effects.log: You tell the whole story. The child listens, and then sweeps, badly, for an hour. You do not correct a single stroke.

events.text: Year after year you have signed at the same ground, and the voice has been saying for weeks that this year's signing pays deep. Three days before year's end, a runner brings word that a friend is trapped in a flooded valley a week's ride away.

choices.text: Go at once; the run can start again

effects.log: You ride. You sign in on a muddy hillside above the flood, the run broken, and you pull your friend out of a roof the next morning. "All those years," the voice says, quietly. "Well. They are still written."

choices.text: Stay three days, sign, then ride

ok.log: You sign the year, take the deep reward, and ride harder than you have ever ridden. You arrive in time, just. The voice says nothing the whole ride.

fail.log: You sign the year and ride. You arrive a day late; others got your friend out, cold and sick and alive. Your friend is kind about it. You are not, to yourself.

events.text: A plague village is closed off by the magistrate's soldiers. They need anyone with medicine or strong qi, and they need them for the whole winter. The voice notes, carefully, that the village is not your ground.

effects.log: You spend the winter carrying water and boiling cloth. You sign in on the village threshing floor. The voice pays a reward it calls "small" and then adds, quite out of character, "good ground, though." (-8 health)
You send thirty taels for medicine. It helps. You sign where you always sign, and the run goes on, and you think about the village every time you hear a cough.

choices.text: Stay; it is not your affair

effects.log: You stay and sign. The run goes on. The voice pays without comment. That spring you pass the village and count the new graves.

events.text: Your run at this ground is long now, long enough that the voice talks about it the way people talk about old trees. And a letter comes: an old friend's child is to be married in the far west, and they want you there. It is a month each way.

effects.log: You go. You sign at the wedding gate in the west, new ground. The run is broken. The wedding is wonderful, and the old friend weeps to see you.

choices.text: Send a fine gift and your regrets

effects.log: You send a jade comb and a long letter. The run holds. Years later the child, grown, tells you the letter was read out at the feast.

events.text: A child has fallen through the ice of the river below your ground, on the very last evening of the year. You are on your ground. The river is not. The voice says, fast, "There is time to do both, probably."

choices.text: Run for the river and do not count

ok.log: You are on the ice before you finish thinking. You pull the child out. You sign, soaked and shaking, on the riverbank at midnight, and the voice says, "Probably was correct."

fail.log: You get the child out and go through yourself. A fisherman hauls you both up with a pole. You sign nowhere; the voice signs for you, on the riverbank, while you shiver. (-10 health)

choices.text: Shout for help from where you stand

effects.log: You shout and shout. Two farmers get the child out. You sign at your ground as the year turns. The voice pays, and you do not look at the reward for a long time.

events.text: The sect is sending a party to escort grain to a famine county, and they are short one fighter. It would mean signing in on the road for a year, away from the ground where your run has grown deep.

effects.log: You go. You sign at a ruined granary in the famine county. Ding: it pays oddly well, the voice admits, as if hunger made the ground hungry to give.
You stay. The run holds. The escort comes back thinner and prouder. You listen to their stories with a feeling you do not like.

events.text: The voice has a confession. "I said the run was precious," it says. "It is. But you have been choosing it over people for years now, and the register is getting... thin. Places with nobody in them."

choices.text: Promise to choose people next time

effects.log: "Good," says the voice. "I will still complain." It does. But next time someone needs you, it is the voice that reminds you first.

choices.text: Say the ground is all that lasts

effects.log: "Perhaps," says the voice. It pays you well that year. It is very polite to you, for a long time afterwards, the way one is polite to strangers.

events.text: You meant to have a quiet trade, with an account book and a steady wage. Then the year's sign-in pays out, not in taels, but in a battered sword manual with the corners eaten by mice, warm in your hands.

effects.log: You read it by lamplight for a year. By spring you can do things with a stick that make the shop boys stare. Your account book, if you ever had one, gathers dust.
You sell it for thirty taels. The voice says nothing, and next year pays you, pointedly, another manual. You start to suspect it has a plan for you.

events.text: The voice pays you a pot of pills and a slip of paper: "Recommended: medicine." You know nothing about medicine. Then your neighbour's child falls ill, and you look at the pot, and at the slip.

choices.text: Try the pills on the fever, carefully

ok.log: You read the pills' smell and colour the way the slip says and give half of one. The fever breaks. By summer half the street brings you its coughs.

fail.log: You give the wrong one. Nothing happens, thank the heavens. A real physician comes and the child recovers. You go and ask the physician to teach you.

choices.text: Take the child to a real physician

effects.log: You pay the physician five taels. The child recovers. The voice remarks that the next pot will come with better instructions.

events.text: For years now the sign-in has mostly paid you in Charm: smiles, a better voice, people stopping to talk. The voice clears its throat. "The register suggests a career where people listen to you."

choices.text: Become a storyteller in the market

effects.log: You tell stories by the well. Crowds come. Fifteen taels in a week, more than your family made in a month. The voice demands, as its fee, that every story have a System in it.

choices.text: Ignore it, and keep to the sword

effects.log: "Your choice," it says. The sign-ins go on paying Charm. You become the most pleasant swordsman in the county, which is not nothing.

events.text: The year's reward is a map. Not a treasure map; a map of the next province, with one valley shaded in, and the words, in the voice's neat hand: "Unsigned ground. Very unsigned."

effects.log: You go. The valley is empty but for an old hermit's hut with a manual on a shelf and a note: whoever finds this may have it. Ding, says the voice, delighted.
You burn it in the stove. The voice is silent, then says, "I can make another," and does, every year, until you go just to stop it.

events.text: The reward this year is an introduction. A letter, sealed, in a hand nobody in the county can read, addressed to the gatekeeper of a sect you had never heard of. The voice says, "Go and see."

choices.text: Take the letter to the sect

effects.log: The gatekeeper reads it, goes pale, and gives you a copy of the founder's practice notes. They will not let you in. They are very polite about it. They ask who wrote the letter, and you cannot answer.

choices.text: Keep the letter sealed in a box

effects.log: You keep it. Some years later you open the box and the letter is gone, and in its place are three taels and a note: "Postage refunded."

events.text: You are good, now, at the thing the System has been paying you for all these years. Better than good. And you realise, sitting in the evening, that you never chose it. The voice is waiting to see what you say.

effects.log: "You chose every year where to stand," it says. "I only paid. The road is yours." You are not sure that is true. You decide it is.

choices.text: Choose something else for a while

effects.log: You spend a year learning to farm, badly. The voice pays out a hoe. Then a better hoe. You laugh until you cry and go back to the sword with a lighter heart.

events.text: You are in the middle of a duel, sword up, when the voice says DING, very loudly, inside your skull, and announces that a reward from three years ago has finally been processed.
events.arc: Ding, at the Worst Possible Moment

ok.log: You keep your eyes on the blade and win. Afterwards the voice apologises, and the reward turns out to be a fine one, which it says is "for the inconvenience".

fail.log: You flinch at the ding and take the flat of a sword across the ear. The reward is a healing salve. The voice says this is, admittedly, ironic. (-6 health)

choices.text: Ask the opponent for a short pause

effects.log: "Pause?" They stare at you. You stare back. They are so baffled they agree. You stand there in silence while the voice reads you a list. The duel, when it resumes, is very awkward.

events.text: You are being examined for entry to the inner court, alone before three elders, and the voice chooses this moment to pay out a backlog of rewards. Four pills, a fan and a live chicken appear on the floor at your feet.
events.arc: Ding, at the Worst Possible Moment

ok.log: You carry on reciting as if chickens appear at all examinations. The elders, unwilling to admit they cannot explain it, pass you. One takes the chicken home.

fail.log: The chicken gets out. The examination ends with three elders and you on your hands and knees under a table. You pass the next year, and they never quite forget.

choices.text: Say it is a trick you have been practising

effects.log: "A trick," an elder says. "Do it again." You cannot. The voice will not. You are told to come back next year with better tricks.

events.text: You are hiding behind a screen from an assassin, holding your breath, perfectly still, when the voice says ding. You are almost certain only you can hear it. Then a little gold coin drops out of the air and rings on the floor.
events.arc: Ding, at the Worst Possible Moment

choices.text: Throw the coin across the room

ok.log: You flick the coin to the far corner. The assassin turns, and you are out of the window. The voice is very quiet for a week.

fail.log: The assassin is not fooled. You get out of the window anyway, but slower, and with a cut down your arm. (-8 health)

ok.log: You come through the screen fast. It is short and ugly and you win. The voice, very small: "I will add a quiet setting."

fail.log: You come through the screen and the assassin is ready. You get away, barely. (-12 health)

events.text: You are kneeling before an old friend's grave, at the funeral, in total silence among the mourners, when the voice cheerfully announces that the graveyard is new ground and asks if you would like to sign in.
events.arc: Ding, at the Worst Possible Moment

effects.log: You think NO so loudly that the voice goes quiet for the rest of the year. It signs you, at year's end, somewhere else, without comment. Later it says, "That was badly done. I am sorry."
You lay your palm on the earth as if in prayer. Ding, very softly. Your friend is in the register now. It seems, somehow, a thing they would have liked.

events.text: Someone is confessing to you that they have liked you for years, very nervously, under a plum tree in bloom, and the voice says, loudly, "DING. CHARM PLUS TWO. ACHIEVEMENT: SOMEONE NOTICED."
events.arc: Ding, at the Worst Possible Moment

effects.log: You laugh, and then have to explain that you are not laughing at them, and the explanation is long and impossible, and by the end both of you are laughing. It is not a bad beginning.

ok.log: You keep your face. You answer honestly. The voice, chastened, does not speak for the rest of the spring.

fail.log: Your face does something strange. They ask if you are well. You say yes. They do not believe you. Neither does the voice.

events.text: You are bowing to the emperor's envoy on the steps of the magistrate's hall, before half the county, when the voice pays out the deep reward for ten years in a row at this ground. You feel your bones creak and settle, audibly.
events.arc: Ding, at the Worst Possible Moment

choices.text: Rise slowly, as if nothing happened

effects.log: You rise. The envoy, who heard your knees crack like firecrackers, decides it was a sign of deep respect. You are mentioned in a report.

choices.text: Steady yourself on the envoy's arm

effects.log: The envoy holds you up. "Are you well?" "Never better," you say, entirely truthfully. You become, oddly, friends.

events.text: {npc}, an inspector from the provincial office, is going through the county's records for something else entirely and has found you: a person who grows stronger every year at the turn of the year, regular as a calendar. {npc} has come to ask you about it, politely.

choices.text: Say it is a family breathing method

ok.log: {npc} writes it down. "A family method," {he} says, "with remarkable punctuality." {He} leaves. You have the feeling {he} will be back.

fail.log: {npc} smiles. "Of course," {he} says. "And next year I will come to watch." {He} means it.

effects.log: You give {him} tea and nothing else. {npc} drinks it, thanks you, and leaves a card. "In case you ever wish to explain."

events.text: {npc} the inspector has come back, as promised, on the last night of the year, and is sitting across from you at the inn, watching. The year will turn in an hour. You need to sign somewhere.

ok.log: You lay your palm flat on the floor under the table while pouring {him} wine with the other hand. Ding. {npc} watches your face and sees nothing. {He} leaves at dawn, frowning.

fail.log: {npc} sees your hand go down and your face change. {He} writes for a long time. "Thank you," {he} says. "That was very instructive."

choices.text: Let the System sign for you

effects.log: You do nothing. At midnight the voice signs for you, and something in your shoulders settles. {npc} stares at your shoulders. "There," {he} says, very softly. "Just there."

events.text: {npc} has put it together. {He} lays out on the table every place you have been on every year's end for years, from witnesses, inn books and one very talkative ferryman. "You are signing in," {npc} says. "For whom?"

effects.log: You tell {him}. {npc} is quiet for a long time. Then {he} burns the papers in the lamp, one by one. "There are people in the capital," {he} says, "who would put you in a cellar and count your years for you. They will not hear it from me."

ok.log: You laugh so convincingly that {npc} begins to doubt the ferryman. {He} closes the case as "eccentric local".

fail.log: {npc} does not laugh. "Fine," {he} says. "Keep it. But I will not be the last one to notice."

events.text: Men from the capital have come asking about "persons of unnatural regularity". {npc} the inspector, your friend now, rides through the night to warn you.

effects.log: You are gone by dawn. You sign that year at a mountain shrine three provinces away. {npc} sends you one letter: "They found an eccentric local. Makes very good tofu."

ok.log: You meet them with tea and a dull, plausible story about your family's breathing method. They leave bored. {npc} drinks with you after, laughing.

fail.log: They question you for two days. They find nothing, because there is nothing to find, but you come out thin and shaking. {npc} is waiting outside with a horse. (-6 health)

events.text: An old shaman in the hills looks at you once across a fire and says, flatly: "You have a clerk. Up there. With a brush. Does it eat?"

choices.text: Ask if the shaman has met one before

effects.log: "Twice," says the shaman. "One clerk was kind. One kept the host alive two hundred years and counted every one." Your voice is very quiet that night.

choices.text: Offer the clerk a rice cake on the fire

effects.log: You put a rice cake on the stone by the fire. It is gone in the morning. Ding, says the voice, and will not say whether it ate it.

events.text: A child in your street has decided you are a ghost, because nobody grows stronger without practising and you never practise. The child follows you around with a peach branch and a very serious face.

choices.text: Pretend to be scared of the peach branch

effects.log: You yelp and run whenever the branch comes near. The child is enormously proud. The whole street is in on it within a week.

choices.text: Explain that practice is not always visible

effects.log: The child listens with narrowed eyes, then hits you with the peach branch anyway, to be sure. Ding, says the voice. "Peach wood," it says, pleased.

events.text: The voice has discovered festivals. It wants to know what the Lantern Festival is, why people eat sweet rice balls, and whether a lantern counts as ground if you are standing under it.
events.arc: The Register Has a Sense of Humour

choices.text: Take it to the festival and explain everything

effects.log: You spend the night explaining lanterns to a voice in your head. It is the best festival of your life. It decides that the sweet rice balls are "excessive but correct".

choices.text: Tell it to read about it

effects.log: "I have no eyes," it says. "Only a register." It sulks until the next day, then asks about dumplings.

events.text: This year's reward is a live goose. You were hoping for a pill. The goose has views on you, and makes them known.
events.arc: The Register Has a Sense of Humour

effects.log: The goose guards your door with violent devotion. Two thieves are bitten that year. The voice says the goose was "a rare grade-two guardian" and will not say whether it is joking.
Eight taels. The goose bites the buyer. The buyer bites... no. The buyer complains. You leave quickly.

events.text: You sign in at the bathhouse, which you thought was clever. The voice says it was clever. The reward is a whole year of being very, very clean. You are not sure this is a reward.
events.arc: The Register Has a Sense of Humour

effects.log: You smell of cedar for a year. Rain beads off you. Mud refuses to stick. People who never noticed you begin sitting next to you.
"You chose the ground," it says. "I paid the ground." You cannot argue with this, and it knows.

events.text: The voice has found out that other Systems exist. It has heard (it will not say how) of a Devouring System and a Sect Lord System, and it would like you to know that it, personally, has never asked a host to eat anything.
events.arc: The Register Has a Sense of Humour

choices.text: Reassure it that it is your favourite

effects.log: "Naturally," it says. It is pleased for a week and pays the next sign-in with a small extra flourish: a sweet in red paper.
Long silence. Then: "Less. Much less. Consistently less." It sounds very much like someone who does not know.

events.text: Somehow, without meaning to, you have signed in at the same noodle stall on the last night of the year, year after year. The owner has noticed you come every year at midnight, put your palm flat on the counter, and eat. The owner thinks it is a blessing.
events.arc: The Register Has a Sense of Humour

effects.log: The owner refuses your money every year after. The stall becomes famous for lucky noodles. The voice is, technically, a co-owner.
The run pays deep in time. You are possibly the only master in history whose great breakthrough smelled of spring onions.

events.text: The voice has started giving you ratings. Of places. "The bridge: four out of five. The inn: two, the floors creak. Your own house: three, but sentimental."
events.arc: The Register Has a Sense of Humour

effects.log: "A five," it says, "is somewhere you have never been and will remember forever." It refuses to say more. You start travelling just to find out.
"Two out of five," you say. "Talks during funerals." There is a long, wounded silence. Then, very small: "Fair."

events.text: A thief has robbed you and run off with your purse, and the year turns while you are chasing them through a melon field. The voice signs the melon field. The thief, panting, asks why you just said "oh good".
events.arc: The Register Has a Sense of Humour

ok.log: You catch them by the collar among the melons and get your purse back. The melon field pays Body. You both sit down, exhausted, and share a melon.

fail.log: The thief gets away. The melon field pays Luck. The next day your purse is found on your doorstep with a note: "Too strange. Keep it."

choices.text: Let them go and admire the melons

effects.log: You let them go. A farmer, seeing you stand reverently in the melon field, gives you one to take home.

events.text: The voice has caught a cold. You did not know this was possible. Every ding comes out as a small, wet "dig".
events.arc: The Register Has a Sense of Humour

effects.log: You drink ginger tea for it, which is the only way you can think of. It works, or it gets bored of sneezing. "Dig," it says, gratefully, then, "Ding. Ah. Better."
"Dig," it says, with great offence. Next year's reward comes wrapped in a handkerchief.

events.text: The training master has kept a register too: of attendance. You have attended eleven mornings in a year. Your strength, tested at the year's measuring stone, has gone up more than anyone's. The master would like a word.

effects.log: "Privately," the master repeats. "Where?" "At the gate," you say, truthfully. The master goes to look at the gate. The gate does not explain itself.
You attend every morning for a year. You are honestly worse than half the yard at the forms. The master is now even more confused.

events.text: An elder of the outer court has accused you, before the hall, of stealing pills from the alchemy hall: there is no other way, the elder says, to grow as you do without training.

choices.text: Ask them to count the pills

effects.log: They count. Not one is missing. The elder, red in the face, finds another reason to dislike you, and you gain a reputation for calm.

choices.text: Offer to be watched for a whole year

effects.log: Two disciples follow you everywhere for a year. They see you eat, sleep, sweep, nap. At the year's end your strength jumps again. Both watchers ask to be your friends.
You shout. The elder smiles: now you have given them something real. You spend a month cleaning the latrines for disrespect. The voice is outraged on your behalf.

events.text: The sect leader's favourite disciple, the pride of the hall, has asked to spar with you in front of everyone. It is meant to put you in your place: the one who naps against the one who bleeds for it.

ok.log: You win, and the hall goes silent. The favourite is gracious, which is worse for you: now everyone is asking what you are.

fail.log: You lose, and it is close enough that nobody laughs. The favourite says, quietly, "Next year it will not be," and you both know it. (-8 health)

effects.log: "I am not worthy," you say. Nobody believes you, but they cannot prove otherwise. The favourite watches you for a year.

events.text: Two factions in the inner hall both want you: one to show the young disciples that rest matters as much as toil, the other to expose you as a fraud before the sect leader. Both have sent you an invitation to dinner on the same night.

choices.text: Dine with the faction of rest

effects.log: They make you their symbol. A poem is written about you. It is not a good poem, but it is popular.

choices.text: Dine with those who doubt you

effects.log: You eat their food and answer every question with a straight face. By the end they are less sure. One whispers that you must have a great hidden master.
Both factions are offended. Both are now slightly afraid of you. You eat noodles at the gate and enjoy them.

events.text: The elders want to know your method. They have offered you a seat in the inner hall, a stipend and a private room if you will teach it to the core disciples.

choices.text: Teach them to sit still at the same place for years

effects.log: You teach them to choose one place and return to it, every year, with full attention. Most give up. Two do not, and ten years on, they are calmer and stronger than they had any right to be.
The elders are offended and impressed in equal measure. Rumours of a secret art grow. Your sect becomes a little more famous, and a little more suspicious.

choices.text: Take the stipend and teach breathing

effects.log: You teach an ordinary breathing method, well. Forty taels a year. Your students do improve, a little, and adore you. You feel guilty and well paid.

events.text: A visiting elder from another sect has watched you yawn through the morning forms. Over tea, the elder asks your sect leader, quite seriously, whether you are being punished or hidden.

choices.text: Walk past and bow, very correctly

effects.log: The visiting elder watches you go. "Hidden," the elder says. Your sect leader smiles, and says nothing, and enjoys it enormously.
The visiting elder laughs out loud. Your sect leader does not. You are given the gate to sweep for a month. You sign there anyway.

events.text: Before the sect's great examination, three disciples who are sure you cheat have hidden your practice sword, torn your robe and locked you in the storehouse the night before.

ok.log: The lock gives. You arrive in a torn robe with a borrowed stick, pass the examination, and say nothing about the storehouse. The three cannot look at you.

fail.log: The lock holds. You sit in the dark, sign in on the storehouse floor at midnight, and are let out at noon, a day late. You sit the examination next year instead. (-4 health)

effects.log: They are punished. You pass. The sect remembers you as the one who reported people, which is not quite fair and not quite unfair.

events.text: The sect leader calls you in alone. "I do not want to know how," the leader says. "I want to know whether it is good for the sect, or bad for it."

choices.text: Say it is good: you will always stand here

effects.log: "Always?" "Every year." The leader looks at you for a long moment, then nods. From then on nobody in the sect questions you openly again.
The leader laughs. "Honest, at least. Neither do I, about most things." You are given a better room.

events.text: You have asked for the job nobody wants: sweeping the outer gate. It means standing on the same stones every day for as long as you like, and nobody looks twice at a sweeper.

choices.text: Sweep, and sign at the gate every year

effects.log: Your broom learns every stone. Disciples step over you without looking. The voice describes the gate as "lovely, lovely ground".

choices.text: Sweep, but watch everyone who comes through

effects.log: Nobody hides their face from a sweeper. In a year you know every visitor, every grudge, every elder's bad knee.

events.text: A pair of young masters from a famous family come to the gate demanding to see the sect leader. They kick your leaf pile apart for fun. One laughs. "Sweep that up, old broom."

effects.log: You sweep it up. They walk in. On their way out, much later, they find the steps so clean they slip on them. Nobody pushed them. Nobody needed to.

ok.log: Your broom moves twice. Both young masters are sitting in the leaf pile, unhurt, astonished. You help them up and sweep around them.

fail.log: They are better than they looked. You end up in the leaf pile yourself. The gatekeeper finds you and thinks it hilarious. (-7 health)

events.text: Night. The sect is at a feast in the inner hall and the gate is yours alone when a raiding band of masked fighters come up the steps fast and silent. Nobody else is awake to see them.

choices.text: Hold the gate with the broom

ok.log: In the morning the sect finds a heap of masked fighters tied up with broom-straw at the foot of the gate, and the sweeper sweeping around them. Nobody can say who did it. You are asked. You say you found them like that.

fail.log: You hold them long enough to ring the alarm bell, and are badly cut doing it. The sect pours out and the raiders flee. You wake in the infirmary with a broom-handle still in your fist. (-14 health)

effects.log: You ring the bell and the sect pours out. The raiders flee. You are given a bowl of rice for good service and go back to sweeping.

events.text: Years at the gate. Young disciples now tell each other a story: the sweeper at the gate is the strongest person in the sect. Nobody believes it. Everybody repeats it.

effects.log: You let your broom pause, now and then, when a disciple is watching, as if considering something deep. The legend grows. Visitors bow to you. The voice loves it.
You are deliberately clumsy in public for a year. It does not help. The story only adds that the sweeper is very humble, too.

events.text: A great master of the demonic path has come up the sect steps alone, asking for the sect's best. The elders are all away. The gate is yours. The master looks at you, then at your broom, then at your feet, and stops smiling.

choices.text: Bow, and ask the master to come back another day

ok.log: The master studies your feet a long moment, then bows back. "Another day," the master says, and goes. Nobody but you knows why; it was the way you stood on the gate stones, like a tree with long roots.

fail.log: The master tests you, once. You hold, barely. "Interesting," the master says, and goes, and you sit down very suddenly on the steps. (-10 health)

ok.log: Three exchanges. The master steps back, sets a hand on their own chest, and laughs. "A sweeper," they say. "Of course it is a sweeper." They go.

fail.log: It is not close. But you are standing at the end, and the master goes, which in its way is a victory. The elders return and find the gate cracked and the sweeper unconscious on it. (-16 health)

events.text: A new disciple, very young, very serious, has watched you sweep for a year and asked, at last, to be taught how to sweep.

effects.log: You teach them to sweep: the weight in the heels, the broom low, the eyes on everyone. In a few years they are the best footwork in the sect. Nobody but the two of you knows why.

choices.text: Tell them to go to the training yard

effects.log: They go, disappointed. They come back every evening anyway and sweep beside you without being asked. You stop pretending to mind.

events.text: Thirty years signed. The disciples you joined with are elders now, or dead, or gone. The youngest disciples think you are some kind of caretaker. The voice has been very sentimental all month.
events.arc: Signed In for a Hundred Years

choices.text: Stay, and let them think it

effects.log: You stay. Nobody looks at you. It is restful. The voice says, "Thirty years is a beginning," which is either inspiring or a threat.

choices.text: Introduce yourself to the new disciples

effects.log: You tell them you joined the sect thirty years ago. They are very polite and do not believe a word. One brings you a cushion.

events.text: The sect records keeper has found your name on the entrance roll of a year when the current sect leader was a child, and has come to the gate to ask if you are your own grandchild.
events.arc: Signed In for a Hundred Years

effects.log: "Yes," you say. "A family tradition." The keeper writes it down with great relief. You are now, officially, your own grandchild.

choices.text: Say no, and that you are just old

effects.log: The keeper looks at your face, which is not that old, and at your hands, which are. The rumour of an ageless disciple goes around the sect in a day.

events.text: There is a hollow worn in the flagstone where you stand to sign. The sect's masons want to replace the stone. The voice is, frankly, panicking.
events.arc: Signed In for a Hundred Years

choices.text: Ask the masons to leave it

effects.log: "It is a lucky stone," you say. The masons, who have heard the stories about you, leave it. The voice thanks you in a small, shaky voice.
They replace it. You sign on the new stone. Ding. "Same ground," the voice says, slowly. "The ground was never the stone." It sounds as if it has learned something.

events.text: A hundred years. Ding, ding, ding, a sound like a whole temple of bells. The sect, which never quite noticed you, notices now: every tree in the courtyard has dropped its leaves at once, in spring.
events.arc: Signed In for a Hundred Years

effects.log: You sweep up every leaf while the whole sect watches from the walls in silence. When you finish, the leader comes down the steps and bows to you, the first time any leader has.

choices.text: Walk out of the gate for a while

effects.log: You walk out of the gate you have stood at for a hundred years and down to the river and sit. The voice is quiet. "Go anywhere," it says at last. "I will write it down."

events.text: Your first year's end in a cell. Four walls, straw and a scratched calendar. The voice is, unexpectedly, thrilled. "The walls," it whispers. "Look at the walls. People have been here a very long time."

choices.text: Sign, and study the wall carvings

effects.log: Ding. Among the scratched days, a dead prisoner carved a stance, and the cell pays it to you. You practise it by moonlight. The guards think you are stretching.

choices.text: Ask the voice to get you out

effects.log: "I pay," it says, gently. "I do not open doors." Then, after a moment: "But I will make this the best cell you ever stood in."

events.text: The prisoner in the next cell has noticed you grow stronger every year in a place where everyone else wastes away. They tap on the wall, slow and careful: what are you eating?

choices.text: Teach them the wall stance through the bars

effects.log: You teach the stance through the bars, tap by tap. By spring the next prisoner can stand again. When they are released, they leave you their blanket.

They do not believe you. They watch, and the next year, at midnight on the last night, they see you lay your palm on the floor. They lay theirs on their own floor. Nothing happens. They keep doing it.

events.text: The jailer has noticed that the prisoner in your cell gets stronger every year, which is not what a cell is for. The jailer has come to look at you, and is nervous.

effects.log: "I am only doing my time," you say. "Very carefully." The jailer brings you a second blanket and asks you, privately, to be kind to the next jailer too.

choices.text: Say nothing and look at the wall

effects.log: The jailer goes away and tells the others. The prisoners start calling you the Master of the Cell. You are not sure you like it.

events.text: You have signed inside a secret realm, the one signature such a place allows. On the way out, the other treasure hunters are counting their finds and comparing. One notices that you are carrying nothing, and smiling.
events.arc: One Signature in a Hidden Place

effects.log: They pity you all the way back to town and buy you dinner. You let them. The voice thinks this is very funny.

choices.text: Say you found what you came for

effects.log: The rumour is out by morning: someone came out of the realm with something nobody could see. People start following you into ruins.

events.text: The tomb of swords remembers you. A year after you signed inside it, every sword in your town's smithy hums when you walk past. The smith has noticed.
events.arc: One Signature in a Hidden Place

choices.text: Ask the smith to forge you something

effects.log: The smith forges you a plain blade for fifteen taels. It hums in its sheath at night like a cat purring. Nobody else can draw it cleanly.

choices.text: Walk past the smithy quickly from now on

effects.log: You take the long way round for a year. The smith tells everyone the swords like you. Children follow you to see if the knives will sing.

events.text: Since you signed on the island in the fog, you see a little further into mist than anyone. A fishing boat is lost in a sea fog off the coast tonight, and the whole village is on the jetty.
events.arc: One Signature in a Hidden Place

choices.text: Row out and guide them in

ok.log: You row out into the white and find them by their voices and the shape of the fog. You lead them home. The village makes you a feast.

fail.log: You find them, and your boat swamps on the way back. All of you reach the beach half drowned and alive. (-6 health)

choices.text: Light fires on the jetty and call directions

effects.log: You stand on the jetty calling: left, left, now straight. The boat comes in out of the fog exactly where you said. Nobody asks how you knew.

events.text: You have signed in on the roads of two regions now, and the voice has started talking about the others the way a child talks about sweets. "Jiangnan," it says, dreamily. "The coast. The west."

choices.text: Set out for a third road

effects.log: You pack light and go. The voice talks the whole way, about the ground, the hills, the rivers, as if it had been waiting a very long time to see them.
"Another year," it says. "Yes. Of course. I can wait." It waits loudly.

events.text: A merchant caravan heading west is hiring guards. Half the pay is good. The other half, as far as the voice is concerned, is a road it has never signed.

ok.log: Raiders hit the caravan once, at a dry well, and are sent off. You collect thirty taels and the voice collects a very happy signature on the western road.

fail.log: Raiders hit the caravan at a dry well. You are hurt and paid half. The western road is signed, at least; the voice is very gentle with you all the way home. (-9 health)

effects.log: The caravan leaves without you. The voice says the west will still be there. It says it twice, which means it is not sure.

events.text: On the northern road, a herder's family shelters you from a snowstorm at year's end in a round felt tent. The voice whispers that this is the best-smelling ground it has ever signed.

choices.text: Sign in by the stove, and help with the herd

effects.log: Ding. Steppe ground. You spend three days helping drive the herd in through the snow, and the family's grandmother calls you a useful guest, which you treasure.
You tell them about the south; they tell you about a horse that once outran a wolf for three days. The voice adds that horse to the register, as a courtesy.

events.text: Every road in the land is in your register now. The voice has gone very quiet, like someone at the end of a long book. "I never had a host do that," it says at last.

effects.log: "Up," it says. "And in. Places only the strong can stand." It is the first time it has spoken to you as an equal.

choices.text: Go home and sign where you started

effects.log: You go home and sign in the old courtyard. Ding. "Same ground," it says, "but the host is different." It pays you more than it should.

events.text: Your own hall. Your own name above the door. The first year's end, you stand on the threshold of the founder's hall and the voice is so moved it cannot speak.

choices.text: Sign, and say a word for the hall

effects.log: You say a few words to the empty hall about what it should be. Ding. "Ground you made," the voice says, thickly. "I like ground you made."

choices.text: Sign with your first disciples watching

effects.log: Your disciples watch you press your palm to the threshold and assume it is a sacred rite. It becomes one. Every founder after you does it, not knowing why.

events.text: A disciple of yours is struggling: years of effort, no progress, and in despair. They have seen you grow stronger without seeming to try and begun to think talent is everything.

effects.log: You tell them about the voice. The disciple stares, then laughs, and laughs, and goes back to training with something lifted from them. "So it was never fair," they say. "Good. Then I am doing it the hard way, on purpose."

choices.text: Train beside the disciple for a year

effects.log: You train with them every dawn for a year. At the end they have improved, and so, to your surprise, have you, in a way no register pays for.

events.text: Rumour among the other sects: the founder of your sect has a hidden treasure in the founder's hall, because the founder visits it on the last night of every year alone. A thief has been caught on your roof.

choices.text: Let the thief see the empty hall

effects.log: You walk the thief in and show them: an empty hall, a worn threshold. "That is all," you say. The thief does not believe you, and spreads the story wider. Your sect gets more applicants.

choices.text: Hand the thief to the magistrate

effects.log: The magistrate thanks you. The rumour grows anyway: now there is a treasure worth guarding. Two more thieves come the next year.

events.text: Ding. A new year signed. The voice reads out the reward in its usual tone and adds, as it does some years, a small remark about the weather on the day you signed.

effects.log: You agree it was cold. It agrees you agree. It is a small thing. It is a good thing.

choices.text: Ask it to read you an old year

effects.log: It reads you a year from long ago, a place you had forgotten. You remember it now, all of it, as if you were there.

events.text: A child asks you why you always touch the ground on the last night of the year. Their family has been watching from across the street for three years.

choices.text: Say it is to thank the ground

effects.log: The child goes home and tells the family. The next year, the whole family touches the ground at midnight too. It is a small custom on your street now.
The child is delighted to be told there is a secret, which is almost as good as being told the secret.

events.text: The voice offers you a small deal: if you stand somewhere you have never stood this year, it will add a Vermilion Double Seal to the register. "For the sake of the book," it says.

effects.log: You sign on a hilltop you have walked past a hundred times. The voice adds the seal with a flourish: your next sign-in pays twice.
"Steady," it says, approving despite itself. The run holds.

events.text: You dream of the register again. This time you are allowed to hold the brush, and write one line yourself.

choices.text: Write the name of someone you love

effects.log: You write the name. The voice says nothing, but in the morning the reward is wrapped in red, as for a celebration.

choices.text: Write a place you want to go

effects.log: You write the place. The voice reads it and hums. That year every road seems to lean that way.

events.text: Ding. "A quiet year," the voice says. "Nothing happened. Nobody died. You signed. I paid. It was, if you will permit me, very nice."

effects.log: It was very nice. You sit with that for an evening, which is rarer than any pill.

choices.text: Say you want more from life

effects.log: "Then go and get it," it says. "I will write it down when you do."

events.text: Ten years signed. The voice paid you something rare, and you feel the heavens' favour on you like warm weather. An old scholar at a roadside stall squints at you and says, "Ten years of something. What have you been counting?"

effects.log: "Years," the scholar says. "Good. Most people count other things: money, grudges." The scholar gives you a book for nothing and tells you to keep counting.
"You walk like a person keeping a promise," the scholar says. "It takes ten years to get that walk."

events.text: Since the tenth year your next breakthrough is favoured, and the voice reminds you of it constantly, like a relative who has paid for your school.

effects.log: You sit in closed practice for a month. Something in you creaks open further. The voice cheers like a crowd. (-4 health)
"The favour keeps," it admits grudgingly. "It is not milk." You take your time. It is the right choice, and it hates that.

events.text: Thirty years signed, and the System paid you something from the world below's old treasures. A collector has heard of it, somehow, and has come with a chest of silver.

effects.log: The collector leaves angry and returns the next year with more silver, and the year after. You come to enjoy the visits.

choices.text: Invite the collector to tea and talk about old things

effects.log: You spend the afternoon talking about old treasures. The collector leaves with nothing but is happy, and sends you a scroll painting at New Year.

events.text: A Sign-In host is a rare thing. A wandering master who heard of your thirty years comes to ask, plainly: "Was it worth it? Thirty years standing where the voice wanted?"

choices.text: Say the voice never chose; you did

effects.log: The master nods slowly and goes away thinking. Years later you hear the master teaches that line to their students.

choices.text: Say some years yes, some no

effects.log: "Honest," the master says. "Like anyone's life, then." You drink tea together until dark.

events.text: At New Year, an aunt has noticed that you came home taller, stronger and better-mannered every single year, and wants to know your secret, loudly, at the table.

effects.log: The aunt does not believe you for one moment, but cannot prove otherwise, and spends the year telling the village about your clean living.
Every cousin in the family takes up foraging. Nobody gets stronger. Everyone eats very well.

events.text: A cousin who has been working the fields all year while you wandered the county demands to know why your harvests come up better than theirs, when you are never there.

choices.text: Share the year's reward with the cousin

effects.log: You give them ten taels and a bag of good seed. They are mollified, mostly. Next year their harvest is the best in the village, which you suspect the voice had something to do with.

choices.text: Help in the fields for a season

effects.log: You work the fields with them for a season. Your hands blister. The cousin forgives you and says you are hopeless with a hoe.

events.text: {npc}, your oldest friend, who knows you better than anyone, has finally said it aloud: "There is something talking to you. I have seen you answer it."

effects.log: You tell them everything. They are quiet, then they laugh. "I knew it," they say. "Nobody naps that much and wins."
"Liar," they say, fondly. They never mention it again, and keep your secret better than you do.

events.text: {npc}, who knows your secret, wants to sign in somewhere with you this year, just to see what happens. They have picked the top of the old pagoda.

ok.log: You climb by moonlight and sign at the top. Ding. The voice asks you to say hello to your friend for it. You do. Your friend nearly falls off the pagoda.

fail.log: You get halfway up, slip, and both end up in the monks' cabbage bed. You sign there. The voice calls it "crunchy ground". (-5 health)

effects.log: You sign on the pagoda steps instead. Your friend is disappointed, then delighted when you pass on the voice's wishes for a happy new year, in its own small dignified words.

events.text: A charlatan in the market is selling "Sign-In Charms": stand on one at year's end and the heavens will pay you. Two coppers each. Half the market is buying. You know exactly how much the heavens care about paper.

ok.log: You stand on a charm in front of everyone and loudly announce nothing has happened. The crowd laughs. The charlatan packs up and refunds half.

fail.log: The crowd sides with the charlatan: it is not year's end yet, obviously. You walk away to jeers.

effects.log: At year's end you sign on the charm. Ding. The voice pays out a dried plum. "For the paper," it says. "Out of pity."
People will buy hope. Two coppers is a cheap hope. You let it be.

events.text: The charlatan has heard rumours of a real Sign-In master and has guessed it might be you. They come to your door wanting a partnership: you stand on their charms, they sell the story.

effects.log: They go, grumbling. Next year their charms say "Approved by a Master". You never find out which master.

choices.text: Teach them a real trade instead

effects.log: You find them work with a paper-maker in the next town. They are surprisingly good at it. They send you a fine sheet of paper every New Year.

events.text: A young person in the market has spent their whole savings on Sign-In Charms. They stood on them for three years. Nothing happened. They are sitting on the well wall, very quiet.

choices.text: Sit with them, and tell them about patience

effects.log: You tell them that the only real secret is standing somewhere on purpose. They laugh, sadly. But next year you see them at the well at dawn, every day, training. They improve.

choices.text: Give them back the money they lost

effects.log: Ten taels, from your own purse. They try to refuse. You do not let them. The voice says nothing, which, from the voice, is approval.

events.text: {npc}, an elder known for picking disciples nobody else wants, has watched you for a year and makes an offer: "I do not care how you do it. I want my name next to yours when the world finds out."
events.arc: The Elder Who Bet on Luck

effects.log: {npc} gives you a better room, better food and no questions. In return you visit {him} every New Year. {He} looks at you like a farmer at a prize ox.
{npc} laughs. "Good. Hard to buy. I will wait." {He} sends you a pot of tea every year anyway.

events.text: {npc}'s rivals on the council say {npc} is grooming a fraud. They demand a test: you against three core disciples, one after another, before the council.
events.arc: The Elder Who Bet on Luck

ok.log: You beat all three, the last one barely. {npc} sits back and sips {his} tea as if {he} had known all along. The council stops talking about frauds.

fail.log: You beat two and lose to the third. It is enough; nobody can call you a fraud now. {npc} grumbles that two out of three is how {he} likes it anyway. (-9 health)

choices.text: Ask {npc} to refuse the test for you

effects.log: {npc} refuses it, haughtily, citing tradition. The rivals are furious. The question stays open, which {npc} seems to enjoy.

events.text: {npc} is old and wants the truth before {he} goes. "I backed you for all these years without asking," {he} says. "Now I am asking."
events.arc: The Elder Who Bet on Luck

effects.log: {npc} listens and then laughs till {he} wheezes. "A clerk!" {he} says. "I bet my whole career on a clerk!" {He} dies that winter, still chuckling about it.

choices.text: Say it was always just patience

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time. "Fine. Keep it. That is also an answer." {He} gives you {his} own tea bowl, the one {he} drank from every New Year.

events.text: {npc}'s other disciples, who never had your luck, are bitter. One of them has stolen your sword and dared you to come and take it back.
events.arc: The Elder Who Bet on Luck

ok.log: You take it back without drawing it. The disciple sits in the dust and cries, and you sit beside them, and the two of you talk until dark. They are not bitter after that, or not at you.

fail.log: They keep it for a week, then leave it outside your door, ashamed. You never mention it. (-6 health)

choices.text: Let them keep it a while

effects.log: You let them keep it. A month later they bring it back, polished, and ask for a bout, fairly. You both enjoy it.

events.text: {npc}, a young disciple who has decided you are the greatest secret master in the sect, now copies everything you do: when you nap, {npc} naps; when you eat, {npc} eats. On the last night of the year {npc} watches you very, very closely.

effects.log: {npc} sees you press your palm to the ground and does the same, with tears of concentration. Nothing happens. {He} is undaunted. {He} does it again the next year.
"Go and train," you say. "Properly. Eight hours." {npc} goes, and comes back every evening to report, glowing. {He} improves quickly.

events.text: {npc} has been told by older disciples that napping is your secret, and has slept through an entire season. {He} is now very rested and no stronger. {He} is close to tears.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the napping is not the secret

effects.log: "Then what is?" "Showing up," you say. "The same place, on purpose, for years." {npc} thinks about it, and picks the training yard, and shows up. Every day.
You train {npc} yourself, honestly, all season. You find out you are a decent teacher. {npc} finds out {he} is a decent student.

events.text: {npc} has been bullied by older disciples who say {he} is your lapdog. They have challenged {him} at the gate, three on one.

ok.log: You put all three in the pond, gently. {npc} stares at you as if you were the sun. You tell {him} that next time it is {his} turn, and next time it is.

fail.log: You take all three on, and lose, and stand back up, and lose again, and stand back up. They give up from embarrassment. {npc} carries you to the infirmary. (-7 health)

effects.log: You watch from the wall. {npc} loses, gets up, loses, gets up. The bullies give up from sheer boredom. {npc} has never been prouder.

events.text: {npc} has broken through to a new realm, by eight hours a day, year after year, and comes to tell you before {he} tells anyone else. "I did it your way," {he} says. "I showed up."

effects.log: "You did it without a voice in your head," you say, and then have to explain. {npc} laughs until {he} has to sit down.
{npc} takes it like a sword of office. Years later, as an elder, {he} still keeps it on the wall.

events.text: You are old now. The voice has started reading you the register in the evenings, a year at a time, from the beginning: the rice cake, the roof, the well.
events.arc: The Last Lines of the Book

effects.log: It takes a whole winter. Some years you laugh, some years you have to stop it for a while. At the end it says, "A good book," and you agree.

choices.text: Ask it to read the years you were happiest

effects.log: It picks them without hesitation, all of them, as if it had been keeping a separate list. It had.

events.text: "Where do you want the last line?" the voice asks, very gently. It is the first time it has said anything about the end.
events.arc: The Last Lines of the Book

effects.log: "Wherever," it agrees. "That is how most of the good lines happened."

choices.text: At the first place I ever signed

effects.log: You make the long trip home. The old courtyard, the pillow where the first rice cake was. The voice is very quiet the whole way, like someone holding a cup carefully.

events.text: A child of the house asks you what you will leave them. Everyone knows you have something, and nobody knows what.
events.arc: The Last Lines of the Book

effects.log: You leave them the list: every place you signed in a long life, and what each was like. They do not understand it now. They will walk half of it before they are old.
"Pick somewhere," you say. "Go back. Every year. Pay attention." It sounds like nothing. It is the whole of it.
